title: Guides
description: Prepare an LJSpeech dataset and train a Piper voice with the Kaggle notebook.
headline:
From recordings
to a voice.
intro: The essential steps for preparing voice data and training a Piper model. Kaggle limits can change, so check your quota before a long run.
datasetTitle: Create an LJSpeech dataset for Piper TTS
datasetIntro: LJSpeech is the standard format expected by Piper. Each sentence is a separate WAV file, paired with its transcript in metadata.csv.
step1copy: Use recordings you are allowed to process and redistribute. Sources might include game wikis, media you own, or public datasets.
hfSearch: Find LJSpeech datasets on Hugging Face
step2copy: Create one WAV file per sentence. For automatic splitting or alignment, these tools can help:
tools: Audacity · manual edits for smaller collections
step3copy: Use one line per file. Separate the filename and transcript with a vertical bar; the filename must match the file in wavs/.
metadata:
000001.wav|This is an example sentence.
000002.wav|Here is another training sentence.
step4copy: Place metadata.csv and the wavs/ directory at the archive root.
step5copy: Create a dataset repository, for example user/wheatley-english-ljspeech. Add data.zip and a README.md with this configuration:
yaml:
---
configs:
- config_name: default
  data_files:
  - split: train
    path: data.zip
---
step6copy: Start a thread in the datasets and training channel with the Hugging Face link and the appropriate tag.
trainingIntro: Kaggle assigns GPU quota to your account, and the allowance can vary with availability. Check the counter before starting a long session.
quotaCopy: Kaggle lists a 30-hour weekly baseline, which may be higher depending on demand and available resources. The quota resets on Saturday at 00:00 UTC.
sessionCopy: Kaggle documentation lists a continuous 12-hour limit for CPU and GPU sessions. CPU-only notebooks do not use GPU quota, but their session length is still limited.
acceleratorCopy: Kaggle retired the Tesla P100 on September 15, 2026. T4 x2 remains available in notebooks; choose it for Piper training instead of following older P100 guides.
resumeCopy: A full training run often exceeds a 12-hour session. This project’s Piper notebook resumes from a Hugging Face checkpoint: after a timeout or an exhausted quota, run it again to continue from the latest saved checkpoint.
beforeList: Check your remaining quota in notebook settings, your profile, or the accelerator usage page.
Stop GPU sessions when you are not using them.
Use T4 x2; P100 is no longer available on Kaggle.
footnote: Kaggle quotas, accelerators, and interfaces can change. Always check the information shown in your account before training.
useVoiceIntro: Install Piper, get the two files for a voice, and generate a WAV locally. The commands below use the version maintained by the Open Home Foundation.
installCopy: Piper is distributed as a Python package. Older guides using the rhasspy/piper repository or its binary archive refer to the historical release.
downloadCopy: Choose a voice from the catalogue and download its ONNX model and matching JSON configuration file. Keep both files together; the JSON path is the model path followed by .json.
voiceCatalog: Browse Piper voices on Hugging Face
voiceForum: Search for a voice in the forum
synthCopy: First download a voice from the Piper catalogue, or replace the name below with the path to your .onnx file.
rawCopy: The sample rate depends on the voice. Check voice.onnx.json and change 22050 if needed.
homeAssistantCopy: Home Assistant connects to Piper through Wyoming. Add Piper under Settings → Devices & services, then use the tts.speak action with the Piper TTS entity.
homeAssistantLink: Set up Piper in Home Assistant
nodeRedCopy: The node-red-contrib-piper-tts package mentioned in some guides could not be confirmed in the public catalogue. One option is to call the Piper command from Node-RED’s built-in Exec node; adapt paths and permissions to your setup.
adviceCopy: Quality depends in part on the training data and selected voice. A higher length-scale slows speech; a lower value speeds it up. noise-scale and noise-w adjust variation in the generated audio.
synthCommand: python -m piper -m ./voice.onnx -f output.wav -- "This is a speech synthesis test."
rawCommand: echo "Hello." | python -m piper -m ./voice.onnx --output-raw | aplay -r 22050 -f S16_LE -c 1 -t raw
pythonExample:
import wave
from piper import PiperVoice

voice = PiperVoice.load("./voice.onnx")
with wave.open("output.wav", "wb") as wav_file:
    voice.synthesize_wav("Hello world.", wav_file)
slowCommand:
python -m piper -m ./voice.onnx --length-scale 1.5 --noise-scale 0.667 --noise-w 0.8 -f slow.wav -- "Slow speech."
python -m piper -m ./voice.onnx --length-scale 0.7 --noise-scale 0.667 --noise-w 0.8 -f fast.wav -- "Fast speech."
npmTitle: Use Piper in a Node.js project with pipertts
npmIntro: pipertts brings Piper to Node.js, with file output or in-memory audio. The recommended mode is PiperNativeTTS: fully native in-process inference (ONNX plus a compiled espeak bridge), no Python, roughly 10x faster than the wrapper. Voices (.onnx plus .onnx.json) remain separate files.
npmInstallCopy: The docs specify Node.js 18+ and TypeScript 5+. Native mode needs nothing else: plain npm install is enough. The classic wrapper mode (PiperTTS through python3 -m piper) additionally requires Python and the Piper module. Selecting a catalogue ID can download the model and its config into models/.
npmQuickStart: Quick start with a catalogue voice
npmCustomCopy: For a voice you downloaded manually, pass the ONNX file path. Keep its matching .onnx.json file alongside it; set configPath if the config lives elsewhere.
npmApiCopy: synthesize() returns audio (Buffer), sampleRate, and text; outputFile also writes to disk. Options: speakerId (multi-voice and multi-style), lengthScale (> 1 slows speech, < 1 speeds it up), noiseScale, noiseWScale, sentenceSilence, normalizeAudio, volume, and outputFormat (wav, raw, mp3, ogg, or opus). mp3 and opus have pure-JS fallbacks; ogg requires FFmpeg. phonemize() and synthesizeChunks() give low-level, sentence-by-sentence access.
npmLegacyCopy: PiperTTS spawns python3 -m piper, one process per synthesis: about 10x slower, keep it for environments where the native engine cannot run. Requires Python and the Piper module.
ppIntro: Some voices use the Piper Plus architecture: multilingual synthesis, prosody, and MB-iSTFT decoding. They carry the Piper+ badge in the catalogue and require the piper-plus runtime, not the standard piper binary.
ppStep1Copy: The runtime ships on PyPI. The phonemizer NLTK data is fetched on first synthesis.
ppStep2Copy: The runtime resolves a model name and downloads its files. Catalogue Piper Plus voices stay available from their Hugging Face repositories too.
ppStep3Copy: Same interface as piper: text in, WAV file out. Multilingual voices cover their six languages in a single command.
ppSynthCommand: piper --model tsukuyomi --text "Konnichiwa, kyou wa ii tenki desu ne." --output_file output.wav
ppStep4Copy: Model pages carry the Piper+ badge and show the license. In-browser synthesis stays disabled for these voices: the site runtime only handles standard Piper.
ppHelp: A question about Piper Plus? The Discord server answers.
npmInstallCommand:
npm install pipertts
# wrapper mode only: python3 -m pip install piper-tts
